summary: For ages 6–8: children identify, represent and estimate whole numbers across several linked representations — sets of objects, base-ten blocks, drawings, place-value charts, expanded form, numerals and especially the number line — and translate flexibly between them. The number line anchors magnitude and order, supporting benchmark-based estimation ('about where does 47 go?', 'about how many in this pile?') rather than exact counting alone. Progression runs from placing a two-digit number on a 0–100 line (Tier A, age 6), to representing one number as blocks, a line point and a drawing and matching a base-ten picture to its numeral (Tier B, age 7), to estimating a three-digit number on a 0–1000 line and 'about how many' in a set without counting (Tier C, 7–8).
misconceptions: Treating the representations as unrelated (can build 34 with blocks but can't place it on a line).
Placing numbers on a line by counting marks only, ignoring proportional spacing (47 put just past 0, or bunched near a benchmark).
Believing estimation is 'wrong maths' — wanting to count exactly instead of judging 'about how many/where'.
Misusing an empty number line by assuming equal gaps where none are marked, or ignoring the scale.
Reading base-ten blocks by counting every cube rather than using the tens/hundreds units.

activities.title: Many faces of the same number
steps: Pick a number (e.g. 247) and build it several ways: a set or base-ten blocks (2 hundreds flats, 4 tens rods, 7 ones cubes), the numeral 247, the expanded form 200 + 40 + 7, and words.
Place that same number as a point on a number line.
Change one representation and update all the others to match so they always show the same quantity (e.g. add one tens rod to make 257, then fix the numeral, the expanded form and the line point).
Say aloud why these are all the 'same number wearing different clothes'.
Match a mixed set of base-ten pictures to their numerals and to the matching words.
activities.insight: A single number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, expanded form or words, and you can translate between them because they all encode the same quantity.

activities.title: Estimate on a benchmarked number line
steps: On a 0–100 line marked only with 0, 50 and 100, place a given number such as 47 or 68 in roughly the right position.
Before placing, decide whether the number is below or above the halfway mark (50) and how far.
Read a mark already placed on a 0–100 line labelled only at its ends (0 and 100, no interior marks) — e.g. a mark at about 70 — and say what number it shows and how you decided.
Scale up: on a 0–1000 line with 0, 500 and 1000 marked, place a three-digit number by proportion.
Explain your placement using the benchmarks: 'past the middle, most of the way to 100.'
activities.insight: Numbers have relative size and order; you can locate them by reasoning proportionally from benchmarks (0, 50, 100; halfway) instead of counting every tick mark.

activities.title: About how many? — estimating set size
steps: Look at a pile or set of 30–50 objects for only a brief moment (too briefly to count every one).
Give a sensible estimate of 'about how many', and say what helped you judge (e.g. comparing to a known group of ten).
Compare your estimate to the actual count and reflect on how close it was.
Discuss that a good estimate within a sensible range is valuable maths, not 'wrong' because it is not exact.
activities.insight: Estimating 'about how many' is a real, valued skill: judging magnitude quickly using benchmarks is different from, and complements, exact counting.

checkQuestion: Show a 0–100 number line with a single mark placed at about 70 (only 0 and 100 labelled). Ask: 'What number does this mark show, and how did you decide?' Then give a blank 0–100 line and say: 'Now mark where 40 would go.'
checkAnswer: Reads the mark as about 70 by proportion (past the middle, most of the way to 100) and places 40 a little below the halfway point, using 0, 50 and 100 as benchmarks.
